title: Boosting Adversarial Attacks with Momentum
authors: Yinpeng Dong, Fangzhou Liao, Tianyu Pang, Hang Su, Jun Zhu, Xiaolin Hu, Jianguo Li

pages.title: The Transferability Problem
pages.subtitle: Why most adversarial examples fail on black-box models

blocks.html: An adversarial example is an image with a tiny, carefully crafted perturbation that fools a neural network into the wrong prediction. The perturbation is so small that to a human the image looks unchanged, yet the classifier's output flips completely.

There are two attack settings. In a white-box attack you know the target model's weights, so you can follow its gradient directly. In a black-box attack you do not have the weights, so you craft the example on a substitute model you do control and hope it transfers to the unknown target.

The catch: the strongest white-box attacks tend to overfit the substitute model. They find a perturbation that exploits that one network's quirks, and when you move to a different architecture the attack quietly fails. There is a real tension between attack strength and transferability.

This paper's idea in one sentence: add a momentum term to iterative gradient attacks so the update direction is stable across steps, which escapes poor local maxima and dramatically improves transferability to unseen models.

pages.title: FGSM and its Iterative Cousin
pages.subtitle: One big step versus many small steps

blocks.html: The Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) takes a single step in the direction that most increases the loss. It is fast and, because it is a blunt one-shot move, it transfers reasonably well, but it is weak against the model it was built on.

Read this as: nudge every pixel of the clean image $x$ by a fixed amount $\epsilon$, moving each pixel in the direction (up or down) that raises the loss $J$ for the true label $y$. The $\text{sign}$ keeps the total change bounded so the image stays within an $\ell_\infty$ budget of $\epsilon$.

Iterative FGSM (I-FGSM / BIM) instead takes many tiny steps of size $\alpha$, re-computing the gradient each time and clipping back into the $\epsilon$-ball. This is far stronger white-box, because it keeps following the loss surface.

But iterating is exactly what hurts transfer. Each greedy step chases the current model's gradient, so the trajectory drifts into a sharp, model-specific maximum that other networks do not share. We want the strength of iteration and the generalization of a single step.

Momentum is borrowed from optimization. Instead of trusting only the current gradient, you keep a running velocity that accumulates past gradient directions. Noisy, conflicting directions cancel out; the consistent underlying direction survives and gets amplified.

The new velocity $g_{t+1}$ is the old velocity scaled by the decay factor $\mu$ plus the current gradient. The gradient is divided by its own $\ell_1$ norm first: this normalization matters because raw gradient magnitudes vary wildly from step to step, and without it a single large-magnitude step would dominate the accumulation.

blocks.text: Step 2: step along the accumulated direction

blocks.html: We move by the sign of the accumulated velocity, not the sign of the raw gradient. This is the whole trick. The direction is now an average of many steps, so it is smoother and points at a maximum that generalizes across models rather than one model's idiosyncratic peak.
$\mu = 0$ collapses back to plain I-FGSM. Larger $\mu$ gives the attack a longer memory; the paper finds a decay around $\mu = 1.0$ works well.
Putting the two updates together gives Momentum Iterative FGSM (MI-FGSM). Given a clean image $x$ with label $y$, a perturbation budget $\epsilon$, and $T$ iterations:

items: Initialize the velocity $g_0 = 0$ and $x^{*}_0 = x$, and set the step size $\alpha = \epsilon / T$ so the total movement respects the budget.
Compute the gradient of the loss at the current adversarial image.
Update the velocity: $g_{t+1} = \mu \, g_t + \nabla_x J / \| \nabla_x J \|_1$.
Repeat for $T$ steps; the final $x^{*}_T$ is the adversarial example.

blocks.html: Because each step moves by $\alpha = \epsilon/T$ in the $\ell_\infty$ sense, the cumulative change stays inside the $\epsilon$-ball over the $T$ iterations.

To transfer even better, the authors attack several models at once by fusing their logits before the loss. An example that fools an ensemble of diverse architectures is far more likely to fool a held-out model, because it cannot rely on any single network's weaknesses.
Here $l_k$ are the logits of the $k$-th model and $w_k$ are ensemble weights. Fusing logits (rather than predictions or losses) gave the strongest transfer in their experiments.

On ImageNet, MI-FGSM keeps the near-100% white-box success of iterative attacks while massively raising black-box success rates. Where plain I-FGSM transferred poorly, momentum lifts black-box fooling rates by large margins against unseen architectures.

The qualitative story: I-FGSM is the specialist that aces the home exam and flunks everywhere else; FGSM is the generalist that is mediocre everywhere; MI-FGSM is strong on both because momentum smooths the attack direction into one that several models agree on.

Crucially, MI-FGSM also breaks through models hardened with adversarial training more often than baseline attacks, because the transferable perturbations it finds are not the ones such defenses were trained to resist.

The method, combined with the ensemble strategy, won first place in both the targeted and non-targeted attack tracks of the NIPS 2017 adversarial competition. The competition was the ideal test: attacks had to fool secret defense models they had never seen, which is precisely the transfer setting momentum is built for.
Takeaway: stabilizing the gradient direction with momentum turns brittle, overfit white-box attacks into robust black-box attacks. A one-line change to I-FGSM, a large change in real-world threat.

The broader lesson for defenders is sobering. If a defense is only evaluated against attacks that overfit a single model, it looks safe; momentum-boosted, ensemble-transferred attacks reveal that the apparent robustness was an illusion of poor transfer, not genuine security.
